Grok subscription

Grok subscription inference through the official Grok Build CLI: live ACP sessions per conversation, private Grok home, tool handoff, fail-closed checks and limits.

About 11 min read · 4 sections

On this page
01 Live sessions 02 Private Grok home 03 Tool handoff (one shot) 04 Limits

A grok-subscription provider spends a Grok subscription allowance through the official Grok Build CLI (grok). API keys are never used: XAI_* and GROK_* variables are removed from the CLI's environment. Model choices are never changed automatically.

Two transports share one Grok home:

Transport When History
Live session (default) A request carries a conversation id (threadId or session id) and is an ordinary turn One long-lived grok agent stdio process per conversation; history stays in the process, so a tool loop costs one seed
One shot No conversation id, a compaction/prewarm/memory request, or grokSessions.mode: "oneshot" One grok -p process per request; standalone only

The one-shot path admits only standalone requests. Historical assistant/tool turns and another request for a previously admitted conversation are refused before a CLI starts, rather than automatically seeding full history again. The bounded admission record survives handler upgrades in the process; a full restart resets it, while historical input is still refused independently. An attempt that produced no content and spent no allowance releases its admission, so signing in and retrying the same turn works instead of failing as a replay. A turn that streamed content or was charged keeps its admission; repeating that conversation is refused.

Codex ──request──▶ gateway ──ACP (stdio JSON-RPC)──▶ grok agent --agent-profile P stdio
                      │  ▲                                   │ MCP over loopback HTTP
                      │  └── tools/call held open ◀──────────┘ http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp/<token>
                      └─ yields {tool call, done}; next request answers the held call

Live sessions

grokSessions is optional and validated like copilotSessions:

{ "id": "grok", "type": "grok-subscription", "grokSessions": { "mode": "live", "max": 4, "parkMinutes": 30, "toolWaitMinutes": 25 } }
Field Range Default Meaning
mode live, oneshot live oneshot restores the standalone-only transport
max 1–16 4 Live conversations at once. A newcomer past the cap is refused (capacity); no session is evicted
parkMinutes 5–240 30 A session idle after a finished turn is closed
toolWaitMinutes 1–25 25 A session waiting for tool outputs is closed (never longer than parkMinutes)

Process. grok agent --no-leader --agent-profile <profile> -m <model> [--reasoning-effort <e>] stdio with the private Grok home, GROK_TURN_SUMMARY=false and GROK_TITLE_REFRESH=false (the CLI must not start inference of its own). --always-approve is never passed. The gateway speaks ACP: initialize, session/new (one HTTP MCP server named gateway), session/prompt, and answers every agent request itself; anything but a permission request gets JSON-RPC error -32601. _x.ai/* notifications are ignored.

Profile (mandatory). The gateway writes a 0600 profile in a private 0700 folder before the CLI starts: tools: [search_tool, use_tool], every built-in tool under disallowedTools, and the gateway system prompt plus the caller's leading instructions as its body. Without a profile the 1.0.52 CLI ran native tools with no permission request, so a session never starts without one.

Tools. The session hosts a loopback MCP endpoint on a random port behind a random path token (and an exact Host check). It lists the caller's tools (the same names as the one-shot catalog; Grok calls them gateway__<name>) and holds each tools/call open. That call is the caller's tool call: the request ends with the call(s) and done while the ACP prompt stays pending, and the next request answers the held call with the caller's output. Parallel calls are collected until Grok is quiet for a moment. server/discover and other unknown methods get "method not found".

Permissions. Every session/request_permission is answered by the gateway:

Request Answer
use_tool naming gateway__<tool> that is in the session's catalog allow_once
search_tool allow_once
Anything else (native tool, unknown gateway tool, other server) reject_once, else cancelled

allow_always is never chosen. A session that is denied 25 times is closed.

Continuation. A request continues a session only when its history is the previous history plus the new items: the outputs for exactly the pending calls (no more, no fewer, no unknown ids), or new user messages after a finished turn. Tool outputs followed by a new user message in the same request cannot continue a held prompt and are refused. Any mismatch (edited history, missing or duplicate results, unknown call ids, changed instructions or tool catalog, a forced tool choice on a tool result, a second request while one is running, or history with no session) is refused with HTTP 400 session_continuity_unavailable and a fixed reason (prefix_diverged, unexpected_tail, fingerprint_changed, forced_choice, concurrent, session_missing, parked, tool_wait_expired, session_dead, session_lost, interrupted, shutdown, capacity, ended_store_unavailable, ended_store_full). A refused request never touches the session and the gateway never replays a conversation into a new process. The history may carry a turn's reasoning summary as typed reasoning or as assistant text; both continue the session.

Ended conversations are final. Once a conversation's session has ended (parked or tool-wait expiry, a crash, a cancelled request, gateway shutdown), every later request for it is refused with the same 400, including the original user-only request: it would pay for the whole conversation again in a second process. A failure after the prompt was sent (crash, invalid or malformed ACP frame, protocol violation, closed session) is reported as that final 400 session_continuity_unavailable (session_dead), not as a retryable 502. A sign-in failure (HTTP 401, still returned to the client) releases the conversation only when it hits a session's very first prompt and nothing showed that inference may have happened. The session counts as having observed inference on a finished turn, on any session/update that is not a pure setup notification (available_commands_update, current_mode_update and config_option_update are the setup ones: message and thought chunks, tool_call, tool_call_update, usage, session_info_update and any unknown kind all count), on any MCP tools/call (valid or not) and on any permission request. Signing in and repeating a request that observed nothing works. Anything observed keeps the record, so retrying the original request is refused (session_dead) and starts no CLI: the charged work lives in the dead process. A failure before the prompt (the CLI dies or fails to open a session) spent nothing and stays a retryable cli_failed.

Ended-record store. The record is persisted, so a gateway restart or crash does not reopen a conversation. It is gateway-ended-sessions.json in the provider's Grok home (0700 folder, file mode 0600, written atomically through a temporary file and rename), shared by every process that uses that home:

{ "version": 1, "seq": 12, "entries": { "<sha256 of provider, home, model, effort, conversation id>": { "at": 1793700000000, "reason": "parked", "seq": 12 } } }

Only hashes, a time, a write sequence and a fixed reason code are stored, never content.

Cross-process safety. Every lookup, reservation, closing and release takes the repo's cross-process lock (withPrivateFileLock, the <file>.lock next to the store), reads the file again from disk, and writes the whole file back before it lets go. A process never works from a copy it read earlier, so two gateway processes sharing a Grok home cannot overwrite each other's records. A reservation is an atomic conditional insert: it records the conversation as live only when the key is absent, and otherwise returns the existing record, which refuses the request. Of two processes admitting the same conversation, exactly one starts a CLI. seq is a write counter that increases with every change, across processes. A closing or release whose write fails is kept in memory and applied under the lock before the next operation; lookups fail closed meanwhile.

Live entries. A live entry (recorded before the CLI starts, replaced by the end reason when the session closes) carries its owner, <pid>:<process start time>. A store instance that finds a live entry whose owner is not this process and is no longer running (the pid is gone, or reused by another process) converts it to session_lost with a fresh timestamp before retention is applied, so an orphan is retained for a full period from when it is found, not from when its gateway started it. A live entry of another running gateway process is left alone. A live entry never expires by age.

Retention. Entries leave only when older than 7 days, never by count. Clock guards: a timestamp in the future counts as now (and is rewritten to now); a record 10 times older than the retention (a clock that jumped far forward, or a gateway idle for months) is suspect and kept, and its age starts again, so one large jump cannot drop records written recently. A smaller forward jump (between 7 and 70 days) can still expire records early. The store holds at most 20,000 entries; past that, a new conversation is refused (ended_store_full) rather than an old record forgotten.

Failures. If the file cannot be read (missing is fine; unreadable, corrupt or not a regular file is not), the lock cannot be taken within five seconds, or it cannot be written, a new conversation is refused with ended_store_unavailable and no CLI starts; a request that carries history gets its usual session_missing. To recover from a corrupt file, move it aside: every conversation recorded in it can then start over, so only do that when none of them matters.

Temporary files. The store writes <file>.<writer pid>.<12 hex>.tmp and renames it. A write that was interrupted leaves its temporary file; under the lock, the next write removes this store's own temporary files that are older than a minute and whose writer pid is not running. A fresh one, or one whose writer is running, is kept; other files are never touched.

Lifecycle. A cancelled request, a crash, an unexpected tool call or output outside a prompt, a timer, or shutdown closes the session: the process group gets SIGKILL, the endpoint stops, held calls fail and the folder is removed. Sign-in failures map to HTTP 401 authentication; other failures use the fixed classes below. The group is always signalled, also after the leader exited, so descendants do not outlive a session. A frame that is not a JSON object (null, an array, a number) ends the connection with invalid_stream and kills the process. A cancellation during startup waits for startup to give up, then releases the folder, the endpoint and the process.

Frames and stop reasons. Every field read from an ACP frame is type-checked (error.code a number, error.message a string, result an object, method a string, id a number or string, params an object); a frame of the wrong shape ends the connection with invalid_stream and kills the process. Nothing from a frame is coerced with String(). The prompt's stopReason is mapped through an allowlist (end_turn, max_tokens, max_turn_requests, refusal, cancelled); anything else is unknown.

Telemetry. grok_session events carry outcome (spawned, continued, refused, reaped, crashed, closed, interrupted), missReason and counts (live sessions, tool calls, permissions allowed and denied, tokens). missReason is always one of a fixed list (src/providers/grok-reasons.ts; anything else is logged as other), so provider text such as a stop reason never reaches telemetry. No tokens, request bodies, tool arguments or environment values are logged.

{ "id": "grok", "type": "grok-subscription", "label": "Grok",
  "models": { "grok/grok-4.7": "grok-4.7" },
  "modelMetadata": { "grok/grok-4.7": { "displayName": "Grok 4.7", "contextWindow": 256000, "inputModalities": ["text"] } } }

Private Grok home

The gateway uses its own Grok home, <stateDirectory>/grok-home unless grokHome names another directory. Sign it in once per Mac:

gateway login grok

The gateway runs the Grok CLI's device-code login against its own private home, so the credential never lands in a personal ~/.grok. The same flow is the connection's Reconnect action in the desktop app. To run it by hand, set GROK_HOME to that home and run grok login --device-auth (--device-code is the CLI's alias). A clean CLI exit is not treated as success; the credential file must exist afterwards.

A missing auth.json fails the request before the CLI starts, and a login the CLI rejects mid-run is reported the same way: HTTP 401 authentication, with a fixed message that names the gateway's Grok home. Neither case is reported as a temporary upstream failure, so a retry does not hide a sign-in problem.

The gateway keeps the home private (0700) and rewrites only its managed sections of config.toml: no auto-update, telemetry, memory, xAI-side tools (X search, code interpreter) or session search, Claude and Cursor compatibility (skills, rules, agents, MCP servers, hooks) off, and exactly one MCP server, gateway. Sections the CLI writes itself are kept. A personal ~/.grok login and its MCP servers and skills are never used.

Tool handoff (one shot)

Every built-in tool is named in --disallowed-tools. Grok reaches MCP tools only through its search_tool and use_tool helpers, so those stay allowed. The gateway MCP server lists the caller's tools for this request and never answers tools/call. search_tool is answered inside the CLI from that catalog. A use_tool block naming gateway__<tool> becomes the caller's tool call, with its tool_input as arguments; the request ends and the CLI is stopped. The client executes every tool.

The request fails with invalid_tool_call and the CLI is killed when the init frame advertises any other tool or MCP server, or the stream contains any other tool, a server-side tool block, or a use_tool for a non-gateway tool.

Limits

  • Text only: image input is refused before the CLI starts.
  • Each admitted standalone request seeds its input. The CLI adds about 13,000 tokens of its own setup, so a tiny reply costs about 2 cents of allowance and long tool loops cost much more. grok_cli telemetry records costUsd from the CLI's result.
  • Every tool step adds a search_tool round trip before the use_tool call.
  • Instructions travel as --system-prompt-override and are capped at 256 KiB.
  • Errors map to fixed classes (authentication, rate limit, allowance or billing, temporary failure); provider text is never forwarded.

Verified on 21 October 2026 with Grok Build 1.0.52 against grok-4.7-build-fast: a text reply, and a tool turn that returned one caller call with exact arguments and left no CLI process running. Fixture tests cover the stream and safety rules without paid inference.

Live sessions were qualified against Grok Build 1.0.52 with probes (an ACP session with a loopback HTTP MCP tool, a held tools/call answered seconds later, and permission allow/reject; the same CLI without the profile ran touch natively without asking). The test suite uses a fake grok executable that speaks ACP and never runs inference: src/tests/grok-acp-fixture.ts.
